name: Kerf
tagline: Columnar tick database and array language from Kona's author, with JSON and SQL syntax; open-sourced in 2022.
description: Kerf is a K/q-style system for financial time series: an interpreted array language and a columnar tick database in one small C binary, built by Kevin Lawler (author of the Kona K implementation) and first sold commercially by Kerf Software around 2015. Unlike kdb+, it uses JSON literals for data and accepts SQL-like select statements, which makes it gentler for people who do not read K. Tables can live in memory or be memory-mapped to disk for transactional writes, and it targets trading platforms, feed handlers, log processing and real-time analytics. The complete Kerf1 was released under BSD-2-Clause in 2022; Kerf2, a concurrent C++ rewrite, is public but explicitly incomplete. Commits are occasional.
statusNote: Commercial product open-sourced (BSD-2-Clause) in 2022; occasional maintenance commits since, and the Kerf2 rewrite is unfinished.

scale.notes: Single process; memory-mapped tables can exceed RAM up to the virtual address limit.

apis: Network IPC clients (Java, Node.js, Python, R)
strengths: Vector language plus columnar tick store in one small binary
JSON data literals and SQL-style selects lower the barrier versus kdb+/q
Memory-mapped on-disk tables with transactional writes
weaknesses: Essentially a one-person project with sporadic maintenance
Kerf2 rewrite is incomplete; Kerf1 lacks multi-core concurrency
Tiny ecosystem and few production references
useCases: Tick-data research without a kdb+ license
Log-file and CSV crunching from a REPL
notIdealFor: Teams needing a supported, multi-node time-series platform
